utterances.text: In the village of Orlovci that was between Kozarac and about eight kilometres from Kozarac, maybe seven kilometres, there was a village of Orlovci, and that was the last checkpoint manned by Serbian soldiers. We were not made to show our IDs there, and when I came to Kozarac, there at the turning point for Kozarac, there was a regular police there in blue uniforms that were patrolling left and right from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise these police patrolling in Kozarac itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised a few of them. I do not really know what their names were, but I knew them from before, from passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. Were you then subsequently told by a member of the Muslim police what the situation was with respect to the situation in Kozarac with the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One day, I think that was eight days before the war started, a guy came. His name was Mevludin. I did not -- I had not seen him prior to that. A young man, very young. He came to a house in my village of Brdjani and that was a youth hall where the young people got together, and several young people, several people got there but not many people, and I came and we came inside. There were about 30 of us there, in there, and the man was explaining the things that were happening around Kozarac. He said the following. The Serbs are, the Serbs really played a trick on us in Prijedor and their leadership. We had an agreement that we have a mixed army, a mixed police, and we believed them. We sat down with them and we had a dinner with them, and in the morning when we got up we saw that the whole town of Prijedor was filled with army. All of the Muslim policemen in Prijedor were disarmed and expelled from Kozarac. However, Mevludin later warned us: "Listen, people, we have to talk to Serbs. We have to find a way to make them leave us alone. If you have any weapons, surrender them. Do not be afraid. Nothing will happen to Muslims if they surrender their arms". Some people who had their arms or pistols, they promised they would go home and give them up. Then this is where we split. We left that meeting and I have never seen that man again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next morning was there a radio announcement with respect to the surrendering of arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Over the radio in Prijedor -- but at that time it was not called Radio Prijedor, it was called Serbian Radio Prijedor, because Serbs had entered Prijedor already -- they were informing us and they were saying that some villages around Prijedor had surrendered all of their arms already. They have said that in Kozarac there were 700 weapons, rifles, that were not surrendered. They issued an ultimatum to bring those weapons to the Local Commune and discard it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there at this time a Territorial Defence group forming in the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. TO existed from before, but that it was within the regular JNA, and they had their uniforms, but they had very few weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many people were involved in this defence group that were forming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately, I am not sure, but I know that -- I know that there was not more than 20, at least that is what I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this group have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sorts of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had M48 -- those are old rifles -- and I saw some, actually one machine gun, an old one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they have any artillery or cannons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Or any tanks or heavy armaments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During this period of time was there a change in the television reception that you could receive in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of a sudden TV programme from Sarajevo disappeared, and we had to watch TV, Belgrade TV, and we could not watch programmes from Sarajevo any more. Then after several days there was also a TV from Banja Luka broadcasting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember the content of the television transmissions that were received once you could no longer receive Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember some officers on television, Banja Luka television, who talked about Kozarac, who were congratulating each other about taking Prijedor without shooting a single bullet, and the only solution was to have people of Kozarac surrender their arms and then nothing would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did some of the people respond to this order to surrender their arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many people returned their arms. They took their weapons to the Local Commune and left it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about yourself, did you have a weapon at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never had any kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you and your family do anything to prepare yourself for war at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, other people did. Several days prior to that they started making some kind of shelters. They were digging holes in the basements. I had a neighbour who had a large basement and we decided to hide there if something should happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did the attack on Kozarac commence?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Niemann, I can see from the witness list that this witness will testify about counts 1 and 24 through 28, but it appears that this line of testimony is starting to become cumulative. We heard from a number of policy witnesses, I am not sure how many, I think 13, but my number may be incorrect, and they talked about the same kinds of things. We now are moving into the individual counts and we are starting to hear from each witness say the same things over and over. I understand that you are attempting to prove your case as expeditiously as possible, but we really have heard enough, I think, about this. We have just heard from so many witnesses. For example, yesterday we suggested that we not see the film again, Exhibit 185 maybe or maybe it is 195. But what I am suggesting is that you move more quickly through this line of testimony and get to what it is that this witness has to offer that is different than the many witnesses that we have heard. Can you do that or tell me why we should not move more quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am here, your Honour, I am at 24th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are going to ask him then about the attack, you are going to ask him if he recalls the attack, you are going to ask him whether there was shelling, then you are going to ask him where he was when the shelling took place, then you are going to ask him where he went. I do not mean to be sarcastic, I really do not; it is just that I suppose from your perspective it is hard for a Prosecutor to know just how much should be offered. What I am suggesting is that we listen very carefully to the testimony, take notes, review transcripts and we have a pretty good grasp on it. I am telling you just my grasp of some of the facts that I am sure that this witness will offer us and my fellow Judges, perhaps, even have a better grasp of it. So I am suggesting that in the interests of time that you do not have each witness repeat this same litany of events that led up to it, because we know pretty well. I mean, you are going to show him at some point that plan of Prijedor, of Kozarac. You may ask him, well, I do not know, but you understand my point? Move along. I am just suggesting that it has become cumulative. This is the first I have suggested it, and I just want you to keep that in mind. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): You were imprisoned in Trnpolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you imprisoned in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you get to Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it happened like this. After the initial shelling on May 24th, May 27th, it lasted from the 24th until the 27th incessantly day and night. One could not stick a head outside. On May 27th, it stopped a little bit around 8 o'clock in the morning and then we went out on a hill and we looked around because my village is up there towards Kozara, and I could see parts of Prijedor, Kozarac, surrounding villages around Kozarac, they were all burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, if I could interrupt you. I think we will pick up when you first arrived at Trnopolje camp, if you would not mind? Where were you taken to when you first arrive at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came first to Trnopolje camp I was taken to a room that was located on the west side of the elementary school on the floor. I was placed there with my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The camp at that stage consisted of a school building, did it, and other surrounding buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There was an office to the camp as well, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that actually in the school building area or was it a nearby place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In another place, further from school, it was a different room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it a different building altogether?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was it in relation to the school building itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The office was next to the road, road from Kozarac to Trnopolje railway station, on the right side closer to the railway station, and on the left side, if you went from Kozarac, and before there used to be a store and next to the store there was a medical centre; and then under the same roof there was an office of the military officers that sat there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened in this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a room where military officers sat, and when the prisoner was brought to them he had to tell them what they asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did beatings take place in this room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there a cinema building as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, cinema building was connected to that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time you were in Trnopolje what was this building used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exclusively, that was the main centre for where women and children from surrounding villages gathered, and it was used for women, for children and for the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the camp fenced in or was it an open camp with no fencing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning it was open until women were transported away and then later they put a wire around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the type of wire that they put around it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first they put a wire that was sort of an iron wire and then on top of that they put barbed wired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any guards in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These guards were armed, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What nationality were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were part of the JNA, the police or some other organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning those were reserve soldiers of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the camp were you given food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for the first four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then given food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they brought food just for the children. They brought food for children and then another TV team came with them and they were distributing some chocolates and crackers to the children and TV was shooting that; and what was the most saddest thing, there were soldiers behind and at the same time they were returning that back to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you are saying that there were television journalists there. Do you know where they came from, these journalists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Banja Luka direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the nationality of the journalists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs. Those were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you saying that in front of the television journalists and TV, candy was being handed out to the people and, particularly, the children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then after the journalists left this was then collected and taken back again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was water available in the camp for people to drink?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you have to go to get your water from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to go across to a private house and go across the road and around us were the guards that were sitting on the checkpoints, and there was also a pump there which we had to use to pump the water and then we would stay in line the whole day to be able to get some water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the sanitary conditions, the toilets and so forth, were they adequate for the people that were kept there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So what was done to provide toilets for the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a school and approximately two and a half to 3,000 people could sleep at the school, and then the rest slept outside by the walls and some people made nylon tents and then slept there. There was just one toilet at school and nobody could go there at school because it was all flooded with water, but they made the detainees to dig out the holes in the ground and use that as toilets, as outside toilets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did disease start to spread in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you from time to time see people taken out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to these people when they were taken out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taken out and never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who would take these people out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mostly guards, guards from around there. They had names written on a piece of paper and they called out people to be found from inside, inside and taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this happen at night time or during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened both during the day time and at night, but it was more frequent at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did these people return to the rooms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you had been in the camp about 25 days, did you see an incident with respect to one of the women that were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to this woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an outpatients surgery there and there was a doctor called Idriz, he is a Muslim, but he had no medicines. There was another doctor with him, I did not know him, and children, there were so many children there and women. All these children fell ill. They were taken sick; they were vomiting. A woman, she queued, she was standing on the stairs, and she was waiting to enter the doctor's to help her, to give her some medicine for her child, but as the woman stood there on the stairs two Serbs soldiers on the road, on the other side of the road behind the wire, were talking rather loudly and seemed to be quarrelling. They were standing some 10 or 15 metres away from the wire and all of a sudden a shot was heard. I looked up and I saw a Serb soldier fall, he fell on his back, but the other soldier who remained standing and held a rifle in the hand suddenly turned this automatic rifle towards the inside, behind the wire, and started shouting as if he was, as if he had gone mad, and started firing at people who stood around there. So that with my own eyes I saw how a woman who was holding her child in her hand, he hit her in the stomach so that she fell down and collapsed, but, fortunately, the child remained alive. There were several more people wounded or who received wounds in their legs, in their arms. Then Serb policemen arrived and they managed somehow to overpower him. They tied him and took him away somewhere and they picked up all those wounded and that woman and drove them away somewhere. Then soldiers, that somebody had fired from inside the camp and killed his fellow guard who had stood there with them. Then major control of Serb soldiers who came in began. They searched the buildings, climbed the tops of buildings to see whether anyone had fired that shot from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So there was some sort of an enquiry, was there, in relation to who had fired the shot and killed this woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The allegation was that someone in the camp had shot the soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the soldier who committed the murder told his superior Commander that there was some sniper among men and women who were in the camp and that that person had fired the shot from inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So far as you know was this soldier disciplined in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Later that day after this incident where the woman was shot, were the women and children and men over 60 years of age taken out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were take taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Camp Commander came and said that all women, children and old people over 60 had to leave the camp as a disease had appeared and that they would go towards Banja Luka, that there they would be accommodated in hotels and be given help. Women agreed to that and the columns started off towards the railway station which was some 300 to 400 metres away from the camp. So they were all loaded on to the carriages. It was a train, it was a train intended for cattle. So women and children were loaded on to that train and taken towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you subsequently told where these women were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were at the camp could you hear shooting occurring from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from time to time; all the time. Fire never stopped around the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people who were firing these bullets, do you know what they were shooting at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were shooting for fun. We were inside and it was like music to them and they could not do without it. They were firing shots all around, around the building, at the buildings, wires, electric wires, and all sorts of things that were around.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that people were taken out of the camp from time to time and who never returned. These people that were taken out, did they fall into any particular groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, first the men with some education were taken, so, for instance, managers, professors, doctors or perhaps engineers, they would be called out, and then after them lower ranking people were taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When they were taken out do you know where they were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see them again after they were taken out, the people that fell into these groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the nationality or ethnic group of these people that were taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims mostly and some Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know a Professor Ante, A-N-T-E?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I met Professor Ante in my room when he arrived with his son. I heard people asking where he had come from and he said that he was from Ljubija, from the mine, that he was a Croat, but I did not really get it quite well where he used to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident in relation to this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Professor was a man of a rather advanced age, I think he was retired also, and he had his son with him of some 25 years of age. A soldier came, whom I had never seen in my life before, and stood in the doorway and asked about some Ante Professor. Then he, this one, stood up and said, "Here I am". The soldier laughed and came in and then said: "Well, how are you, Professor?" and the Professor was silent. The soldier then said: "Professor, do you remember me?" The Professor said: "Perhaps." "How don't you? I was a pupil of yours? Don't you remember all those bad marks you gave me?" The Professor replied: "Well, I gave you the marks which you deserved, sir." The soldier laughed again and said, "Well, you see, Professor, had those marks been better your life would have lasted longer, but as it is you have to come with me." So the Professor got up and went out and a minute later while he took him out into that corridor he returned and then called out the Professor's son, I cannot remember his name. The younger man stood up and was about to fetch his coat, but the soldier said: "No, you won't need this." So they both went out and I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from the room you were in or stayed in in the camp, were you able to move around the camp outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not outside the camp. Within those wires after 8 o'clock every day until 7 o'clock in the evening, that was summer time, we could move within those wires.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you were able to associate with other prisoners kept in the camp, that is within the wire boundary of the camp, but what you say is you could not go beyond that, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Shortly after this incident with the Professor, do you recall that lists of names were taken up of the prisoners in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who took up the lists of names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three women who were from the Serbian Red Cross who compiled the list of all those who were in the camp. We all had to go to them and give our name and surname, and were threatened that we would be shot if we did not do that. So that we all queued up and the list was ready in about three or four days time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the list of all the prisoners had been completed, what then started to happen in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this census they began to come again to take out from the camp by name and surname every day, every night, 10, 15, 20, people were taken away in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say, "they" who do you mean by "they" came and took them away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers, Serb soldiers who came through various parts, who were not guards. All of a sudden out of the blue a group of soldiers would turn up with a list and the guards led them in and they moved amongst the soldiers, would find those persons, would take them into custody, tie them and take them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did some of these people that were taken out whose name was called from the list, did they return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did any of the people in your group that were taken out when they were called out on these lists, did you ever see any of those people come back into your room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember a person called Eno Besic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ener?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: E-N-O, Eno Besic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eno Besic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. Eno Besic was in the camp with me, and one day Serb soldiers came to the door and called out his name and told him, "Come with us", and Eno went out of the camp. He went away and then one night, then a day and then another night and Eno was back. He had been to interrogation. Eno could barely walk. When we came up to him he was in a room. He could not breathe. All he said was, "A little bit of water". We did have some water and so we gave it to him, unbuttoned him, and we saw that on his chest they had made a cross and likewise on his back. The pain was excruciating. The man could not sleep all night. He cried. It was very hot. There were flies all around. It was filthy in there. Then a day or two later the man was still moaning and crying and people were trying to move away from him, and when we looked on his back where they had cut this with a knife there were worms, worms, live worms wriggling around, and we tried to take them out with the water and something, but the stench was so horrible that one could not come near him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you interrogated yourself when you were in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you when you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One day soldiers came and called out my name. So I came, I went with them. I came into the office where the camp Commander was sitting. His name was Slobodan Kuruzovic. I entered and I stood before him. He told me: "Turn your chair". I turned the chair the other way round, not as one should sit, and he was standing in front of me. I was holding on the chair with my hands. Behind my back was a soldier and Slobodan Kuruzovic questioned me and said: "Now tell me how many Serb soldiers have you killed? Have you been to war? Very slowly, very nicely, the better you tell us the easier it will be for you. Where did you leave your weapons?" I repeated that I had not been to war, that I had no weapons, and he laughed at me. "They all say that", he said, "You are all alike". All of a sudden I felt a strong blow on my back, so that across the chair I began to fall, but later a soldier straightened me up and told me: "Speak up", but this blow was so hard, I think it was something metal, I think it was a kind of a stick with a ball or something, it was so heavy that I could not breathe, I could not recover. Later a man entered through the door and said: "Stop it". When I looked up I saw my boss, the boss from the company where I had to work. His name was Slobodan Milunovic. He said: "Stop it, I know him. He is my worker. He had no rifle and I guarantee that he had not participated in the fighting," and then Kuruzovic said: "All right, if you are vouching for him, then I will let him go," and the soldier who was behind my back said: "You can go." So I walked out of the room, straight through it. To the right in the corridor was a room that was a battery room. There were no windows there, only a metal door. There two soldiers met me. They put me against the wall and they were pushing me with their rifle butt to indicate where I was to go. "No, you don't go there, you are coming here to talk to us." I entered that room and that was terrible. The walls were all bloody. The ceiling, there was blood on ceiling even, the floor was bloody. At a certain point in time I fainted. Then I regained my conscious and then two soldiers came in and a little while later two more came. They stared at me and one of them said: "Now you come with us and you will find the rifle where you have hidden it, gold and money and then we shall let you go and you have solved all your problems." I said: "I have no gold. I have no money. I have never had a rifle." Another soldier approached and said: "Look at the wall." I looked at the wall. "Do you see the picture on the wall?" There was no picture on that wall, so I said, "No, there is no picture on this wall", and he repeated: "Don't you see a picture on this wall?" "No." Then I was hit again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you being beaten all of this time or some of the time as this was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not beat me during the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After the interrogation when you were put in this room were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that were beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had never seen them ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the nationality ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the nationality of the people that were beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Serbs soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The gentleman that saved you from being beaten when you were with the Camp Commander, Slobodan Milunovic, how was he dressed at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in an army officer uniform. He had his ranks with some three stars and around that was a yellow band. I think it was the rank of the JNA, of a JNA Major, and that is how the soldiers addressed him, Comrade Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about Kuruzovic, how was he dressed, the Camp Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kuruzovic was Camp Commander and this one was another one. This one was Milunovic. He was not an army officer; he was a plain soldier. I did not see any rank insignia on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So just to clarify that, are you saying that Kuruzovic was the one you described as the JNA Major?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the person that was formerly your boss, Slobodan Milunovic, did he seem to be in a superior position to the Camp Commander Kuruzovic from what you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were taken into the other room that you called the battery, did anyone threaten you with a knife or put a knife near you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened? Can you describe how that happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I fell down, when the first soldier hit me, then he put his bayonet here, I still have the scar, and turned it round.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you also hit in the mouth when you were there in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I took a blow on the mouth, a very heavy one, with a rifle, with a butt, and then I did not know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is when you lost consciousness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you woke up did you notice that you had teeth missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I found two teeth in my mouth and another one had fallen out. My jaw was broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think when you said that they put the bayonet to your head you pointed towards your temple, did you, at the same time when the soldiers put the bayonet up to your head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you wake up after this beating, after you had lost consciousness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same room I felt somebody shaking me and I looked up and the same man in an army uniform, he was calling out my name. That man was very familiar to me. We used to work in the same company. I have forgotten his surname but his first name was Djuro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he do with you when he woke you up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He helped me stand up. He took me out and tried to enter my room with me, but as all the prisoners were already there he could not because the staircase and rooms were all full of people, crammed with people lying all around, so he took me back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did he take you to then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took me to a corner of a building where the roof extended over the building and he said: "This will protect you from the rain", and found a piece of rag and wiped the blood off my face and then he left me. He had to go quickly to leave the wire compound quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who the deputy of the camp was, the deputy commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he was a captain by rank and his name was Branko Topola. At the time he was Deputy Camp Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did he act towards the prisoners in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the outset very nice, very kind. He sort of sympathised with people. He said: "Well, I am not a pure Serb. My mother is Muslim. My father is a Serb, but they forced me to be here with you and to guard you", and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Camp Commander ever address the prisoners in the camp and explain who he was and where he had come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once we were told all to line up. He gave us his name. He told us his name was Slobodan Milunovic, and as far as I can remember he said that he used to work in Sanski Most as a professor, a teacher in a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On that particular day did he say what was going to happen to the people in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he explained and warned us that all, to all prisoners: "Here are my soldiers amongst you, and in case one of my soldiers is missing or is killed by you, you will all be shot."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened after this? What did he say to you after this, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say anything about people then being able to leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after that he let us go and the next day he had us lined up again and said: "The convoy arrives tomorrow. I shall set you free, but only those across the road, across the main Banja Luka/Prijedor road who live on the right-hand side of the road, those who have remained without their houses and who have documents enabling them to go to third countries."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did buses and transport then subsequently begin to arrive at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, as far as I can remember, three or four buses arrived and two trailer trucks with tarpaulin and people were ordered to board them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about yourself, did you board the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no chance. There was no way I could board this bus. I had my brother with me and we were looking at what was going on. People were practically losing their lives scrambling for a place on those buses. The buses were crammed and then all the rest were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the day that these buses were there, did you see soldiers in uniforms different to that which you had seen before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time when I saw some soldiers in black uniforms, and they had APCs with big machine guns and they were standing by the sides of buses and trucks, and they were soldiers and we have been told they had arrived from the direction of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did these soldiers then proceed to escort the buses as they left the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30. (1.00 p.m.) (Luncheon Adjournment). (2.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, before the adjournment for lunch today, you were telling us about an address that you were being given by the camp Commander, Kuruzovic, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnic group he was, what nationality he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that you said that buses later came and people were taken away in the buses and you were describing how you saw soldiers in unusual uniforms that you had never seen before, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you later hear something on the radio about what had happened to those buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard that the buses were stopped at the Vlasic Mountain, and that all the detainees that were in the bus were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After hearing this the next day or some period after that, did Kuruzovic then call you out again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he then speak to the assembled prisoners once more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He lined up the prisoners, and said, "Maybe some of you heard about the incident that was announced over Croatian radio, and that incident that was announced over the Croatian radio is not true. It is true that the prisoners, detainees, were released at the territory held by Muslim army, Muslim government. About 20 of them were killed by the Muslims who were shooting".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "the incident over Croatian radio", are you talking about the killing of people on the Vlasic Mountain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After this period of time did the Red Cross then come to the camp, the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened when the international Red Cross arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The International Red Cross arrived to the camp three days after the convoy. Another convoy was prepared and people that heard over the radio that the first ones that went with convoy were killed, people, nevertheless, started loading the buses and trucks. However, while they were loading the buses and trucks, a white vehicle with blue stars came and all of a sudden Serbian soldiers ordered everyone to run away from the buses, and then all of a sudden they disappeared as though they went into the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you are talking about the blue stars, is that the symbol of the European Community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Kuruzovic say anything to the people that assembled there in relation to what the nature of this camp was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that that was not a camp, that this was a shelter, a gathering shelter, a gathering point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In any event, after the International Red Cross had come and the European Community monitors had been there, did things begin to improve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In what way did they improve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, we started, we were being given food in packages and then once a day we were given a cooked meal and they gave us the -- they enabled us to have water inside, so that we could at least have a bath with the cold water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the period of time that you were in Trnopolje camp and before the International Red Cross had come and things had started to improve, do you recall an incident one day when you were ordered to pick up a shovel and to go into a field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do on that day when you were ordered to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For several days we were without food, we were not given any food. They were cooking for us water in which they poured bones from the butcher's shop, and they made a soup for us out of those bones without any salt, and this is what we lived on during the whole time we were in the camp. We needed the bread and a woman, a Muslim, who worked there in the camp with other women from Serbian Red Cross, she decided to take money from some of us that had money and buy bread through those women so that we could get it, and this is what we had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did she subsequently get that bread and did she bring it to the front of the camp? Did you then go out to the front to collect some bread and while you were out there did a soldier order you to move to a particular place where you were told to pick up a shovel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you then go with the shovel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not just me, I did not do this myself. The soldier kept me for several minutes and then the other soldier went inside and took another four young men, aged between 18 to 25, and the five of us, we went above the building where there used to be a cafe, and this is where Serbian Red Cross was in that cafe; and then above that building there was a garden and this is where two Serbian soldiers stopped us, and they measured by steps the area that we were supposed to dig out shaped in the shape, in the rectangular shape, and they told us that the depth of that should be 80 to 90 centimetres. We started digging and the soldiers took the hay and they put it next to a fence. Then they sat down on the fence -- on the hay and they took out a bottle with cognac and started drinking. Then after several minutes two more soldiers joined them. They were terribly looking, they were bloody and unshaven; and while I was digging I had my face turned to them, but I was close to them, and I listened to the conversation that the four of them had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were they talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were talking, they were saying which two of them were supposed to fill in the hole that we were digging out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they say what they were going to fill in the hole with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With -- manually with shovels.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. But did they say what they were going to put in the holes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So what did you do then at that stage, at that point, after you had heard this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood that they had an argument between them so -- I understood that they would fill up what we were digging out, and then I turned towards one of those soldiers and I asked them, since, soldier, there was a terrible dysentery, so that every five minutes we had to run to the toilet, I told to one of them that I had a pain in my stomach, so could he let me go so I could go over there to another garden, and he gave me five minutes, and he said, "Come back after that".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went out of that area did you go towards a barn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got to -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The barn was to my left, and I felt a smell, aroma coming, unpleasant smell, coming from the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you look towards the direction where you smelt this aroma?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I looked and two metres away from me was a heap of people wrapped in something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these people dead or alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dead people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to determine their condition, the condition of their bodies by looking at them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were placed as sardines, one on top of the other, and I saw that their heads were shattered, so that I concluded that they were not killed with firearms; and I also saw above their heads a huge stick that was all bloody, a wooden stick.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: About how many bodies did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to my estimate, I could not count them but around 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw these dead bodies there what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, as I looked to the right, the first two that were next to me, and I saw this first time in my life that their tongues were pulled out and they were tied to each other by a wire. One of them was not older than 18. He was very young.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they all appear to be male or were there males and females?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were only men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they dressed in military or civilian clothes, could you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not dressed in military uniforms; they were all civilians. Some of them were even in red shorts and they only had the shorts, they had no tops on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then make your escape from this place and go back to the camp in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went back to the camp, did you keep yourself inconspicuous for a couple of days in case the guards that had let you go to the toilet were looking for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the whole time I was in the room I had my brother with me and I only told him what happened. He was guarding the whole time and looking out for the soldiers that might approach us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the men that had gone digging with you, digging this big hole, that you had left, did you ever see those men again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then meet the father of one of the men that were digging with you in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he describe his son to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the man crying and telling me, "My son disappeared. He was here in the morning around 8 o'clock, and I do not know what happened to him", and then I asked him how did his son look like, and he described his son and said that he had something under his eye. I concluded that that was the man because I recognised him, the one that was digging with me, but I did not say anything to the old man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "something under his eye", do you mean a birth mark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During your time at the camp, did you ever have occasion to see women being taken away from the camp by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances when you saw this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One day, I do not know remember what date it was, but after I have been at the camp for about one-and-a-half to two months, in the beginning not all of the women were sent away from the camp, and I got up in the morning at 8 o'clock and wherever I looked, to the left or to the right, everyone was crying and that was strange; why were the people crying? And then I asked one of them what happened. He told me, "Would you like to see? Come with me". I went. I followed him into a cinema where mostly women, children and elderly were placed, and he took me and at the entrance into this cinema, I saw to the right there was an outside toilet and this is where two girls were lying. They had very few clothes on them and they were bloody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to assess about how old they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were around 13 to 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then go into the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went into the building what did you see then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered the building and I saw another two girls that were wrapped in blankets. They had no clothes. When I looked to the other side, I saw another girl that was not giving any signs of life. However, a man who stood by me, you know, pushed me into the shoulder and showed me to the right and I saw there were four old men lying and blood all over around them. When we came closer, I saw four men slaughtered. These older men were over 60 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "slaughtered", how were they killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their necks were stabbed with knives and bayonets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the girls that you saw there, did they appear to have been injured in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were bloody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As if someone had beaten them or something of that nature, is that what you are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, beaten or the clothes were pulled from them. This is how they looked, half dead. One of them was not giving any signs of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ask the people in that cinema building what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers came during the night with flash lights. They came from the tanks, and those were the most dangerous in that area. They came in. Inside the guards that stood there moved away, and then they were choosing the girls, women that they liked, and they were taking them out. Some of them defended themselves and they were beaten then. So that people in the dark tried to save whomever they tried to, could save, but all the elderly that were trying to save the women were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember on one occasion on a rather hot day an incident that you saw outside the fence of the Trnopolje camp involving a soldier by the name of Dragoja Cavic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldier's name is Dragoja Cavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Cavic, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you see with this soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw a woman who was carrying a plastic bag. The woman was about 30, maybe 35 years old. Dragoja Cavic, whom I met there for the first time and found out his name there at the camp, was walking towards the woman and was calling her by her name. I do not remember what her name was. He asked her where her husband was, and who was she looking for at the camp. The woman answered, "I have a son, a very young one who is in the camp so I brought him some food". He turned around and ordered the two guards that stood there to find her son and bring him over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this soldier, Cavic, appear to be intoxicated at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers brought the son. Then after that Cavic ordered the woman to say where her husband was, and he said that her husband killed a relative of his, as far as I could understand. The woman answered, "I do not know." Cavic repeated again, "I will kill you". The woman said again, "I do not know".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did Cavic then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came closer to the woman and he put a pistol on her head by her ear, and he ordered her to take off her top, the clothes, the top clothes. The woman was crying terribly, but she still started taking it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She took it off. Then again he was saying he was asking where her husband was, and then at one moment I heard a -- I heard firing and I looked at the road and the woman was lying on her back. He shot her in the head. Then after that her son was screaming so much that you had to close your ears. The soldier, Cavic, turned to this young man and said, "Get undressed, naked, and let everyone see". The boy was crying. He started beating him and pulling the shirt off him. He pulled the shirt off and then said using these words which I never heard in my life, "Now I will make you rape your dead mother". After those words, the people that were standing by the wall of the school, they tried to leave this wall and run inside. But the other soldier with a very cruel voice said, "Sit there and watch and everyone who moves will be shot". We had to watch this. All of a sudden, I heard firing and I looked up and saw as the boy fell next to his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one moment from somewhere the soldiers, other soldiers, pointed their guns towards Cavic and said, "Put your arms up". He threw his pistol away and he still had another automatic rifle on him and he discarded that too. They came closer to him. They put the handcuffs on him and they took him somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see Cavic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next morning when I came outside I saw Cavic in the same military uniform. The same pistol was on him and the same rifle was on him. He was walking by the wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He appeared to be back on duty again, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came back to his duty as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stay in Trnopolje camp for a period of about four-and-a-half months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then forced to sign a paper concerning your assets and property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the effect of the paper you had to sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the effect was that all of us had to sign the document, that on our own free will we are giving our property to Serbian authorities and that we will never come back, neither with the gun nor without the gun; whoever did not sign could not leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you had signed this paper, were you then shortly after that period allowed then to board buses which headed towards Prijedor and ultimately you arrived in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the way to Croatia up until the time when you were taken over by the UNPROFOR were you under armed guard of the Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were under armed guard of Serb soldiers up until Dvor on Una river. This is the entry into Croatia. This is where a large bridge was; and at that bridge halfway through the bridge Serb soldiers escorted us and then they loaded us on buses and returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the accused in these proceedings, Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a long time, but some 10 years before the war, that is when I really got to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember when you met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was somewhere in 74 or 5, I cannot be more precise. That was the first time I sat close to Dule Tadic and a friend of mine invited me to join them at their table.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was the friend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ismet Karabasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the place where you met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was in Kozarac and the restaurant was called Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this occasion did you have a conversation with Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then meet on a second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you come to see him the second time, that you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second time I came about and I saw at the table, at the same place in the same restaurant, I saw Dule Tadic sitting with policeman, Emir. Emir was next to him and he invited me and I sat at their table.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you sat down at the table with Emir and the accused Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is Emir's second name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Emir Karabasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from these two particular meetings that you can recollect with the accused Dule Tadic, did you see him from time to time in the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did he live in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He lived in Kozarac when one goes along the main Prijedor/Banja Luka road and then enters Kozarac, to the right we have a restaurant and beyond the restaurant there was a shop, footwear, and then there was a residential house and then the next one was Dule Tadic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to go past this part of Kozarac on a fairly regular basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it would be Saturday or Sunday, when I was free.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether, so far as you know, Dule Tadic lived in this same house in Kozarac all the time that he lived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while he lived in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what he did, what Dule Tadic did before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What his business was, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any commercial activities associated with his residence in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had a cafe bar below his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know his father's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was his father's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ostoja Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was Ostoja Tadic reasonably well known in the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was known about him, about the history of Ostoja Tadic that you know of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took part in the last war as of 1941, from the beginning of it. He was an eminent citizen of a cheerful disposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was alive at the time of the commencement of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the accused Dule Tadic was married or was he a single man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Married.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where his wife came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the village of Vidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether they had any children, Dule Tadic and his wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you how many children they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know any people who were associates or friends of Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really, well, one, there was one whom I often saw with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Policeman, Emir Karabasic. That, I think, was his closest friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know his wife's father's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether Dule Tadic was involved in or interested in any sporting type activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was, to your knowledge, Dule Tadic reasonably well known in the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know why he was reasonably well known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he was the best known among children and young people who always looked up at him and pointed at him, "There's Dule Tadic and he coaches karate".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I would like to move on to a part of the evidence which relates to the application that I made yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for five minutes and then we will go into closed session. (The court adjourned for a short time) (Closed Session)
